fatal_errors: The targeted property is misidentified: the paper concerns enhancement of coercive field in fcc Fe-Co-Ni-derived high-entropy alloys, not suppression of saturation moment.
The proposed CoCrFeMnNi single-phase system does not reconstruct the dual-phase FeCoNiTi material containing fcc and C14 Laves phases.
The central intervention and comparison—rapidly quenched dual-phase FeCoNiTi versus a compositionally matched C14-dominant alloy—are absent.
The proposed longitudinal-spin-fluctuation mechanism conflicts with the target mechanism involving fcc/C14 coexistence, antiferromagnetic coupling to Ti, spin canting, and domain-wall pinning.
The cited evidence discusses spin fluctuations, phase stability, and stacking-fault energy in CoCrFeMnNi but does not establish orbital-moment decoupling or suppression.
The predicted cryogenic negative stacking-fault energy is unrelated to the reported high coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K and the multiple magnetic transitions.
explanation: The response only broadly aligns with the topic of magnetism in fcc 3d-transition-metal HEAs. It misses the specific Fe-Co-Ni-Ti dual-phase material family and the property sought: coercivity exceeding the roughly 100 Oe limit typical of single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys. The relevant scientific challenge is explaining how the normally small orbital-moment contribution can nevertheless contribute to unusually high coercivity when the fcc phase coexists with a C14 Laves phase and spin-canted/domain-wall-pinning effects. Instead, the hypothesis substitutes a different Cantor-alloy problem centered on longitudinal spin fluctuations, saturation moment, and stacking-fault energy. Although the proposed XMCD experiment could test its own orbital-moment claim, that claim is not supported by the supplied evidence and does not discriminate the target dual-phase mechanism.
